prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "MARRIOTT INTERNATIONAL INC /MD/" (ticker MAR), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MAR", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Marriott International, Inc.
markets: Luxury hotels (Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis, JW Marriott, W, EDITION, Bulgari, Luxury Collection)
Premium full-service hotels (Marriott, Sheraton, Westin, Renaissance, Le Meridien, Autograph Collection)
Select-service and extended-stay hotels (Courtyard, Fairfield, Residence Inn, SpringHill Suites, Element, Four Points, citizenM)
Midscale hotels (City Express by Marriott, Four Points Flex, StudioRes, Series by Marriott)
All-inclusive resorts, timeshare licensing and residences
Loyalty and co-branded credit cards (Marriott Bonvoy), Homes & Villas, Apartments and outdoor lodging

mission.statement: Connecting People Through The Power of Travel
mission.source: Marriott Serve 360 ESG progress report 2024 (stated as the company's purpose; Marriott publishes it as a purpose rather than a formal mission statement)
mission.plain: Marriott wants travel and its hotels to bring people together.

about.plain: Marriott runs the world's biggest family of hotel brands, like Marriott, Courtyard, Sheraton, Westin and Ritz-Carlton. It mostly does not own the buildings: other people own the hotels and pay Marriott fees to use its names, booking system and Marriott Bonvoy rewards program, or to run the hotel for them. At mid-2026 its system had 10,082 hotels and about 1.81 million rooms. It also earns money when banks issue Marriott Bonvoy credit cards.
about.customers: Travellers on vacation or business trips book its rooms, while hotel owners and developers pay it fees to carry its brands.
about.everyday: If you have ever stayed at a Courtyard, Sheraton, Westin or Ritz-Carlton, or collected Marriott Bonvoy points, you have used Marriott.

money.plain: owners repaying hotel staff, marketing and reservation costs Marriott pays for them (little profit)
fees for using its brand names, plus credit card branding and timeshare licence fees
room and other revenue from hotels it owns or leases
a cut of sales for running hotels for owners
a share of hotel profits when managed hotels do well

money.part: New lodging formats (midscale brands, citizenM, Apartments, outdoor lodging, Homes & Villas)
money.plain: fees from newer brands and stay types added since 2023

result.summary: Yes: Marriott has a wide moat built on the largest hotel brand portfolio in the world, the Marriott Bonvoy loyalty program (nearly 271 million members at end-2025 and more than 295 million by mid-2026), and the scale of its reservation and distribution system. Owners pay fees to join because Marriott-branded hotels win more direct bookings and loyalty guests, and its record pipeline of about 629,000 rooms locks in years of fee growth. The advantage is durable, though Hilton, IHG, Hyatt and Airbnb compete hard for both owners and guests.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross fee revenues rose 5.2% to $5,438 million in 2025 while worldwide RevPAR grew only 2.0% (U.S. & Canada +0.7%), showing fee growth comes from adding rooms (net rooms +4.3%) and credit card fees more than from raising room rates; in Q2 2026 worldwide RevPAR rose 3.4% and the company signed new long-term U.S. co-branded card deals with JPMorgan Chase and American Express.

moats.evidence: Owns 30-plus brands from Ritz-Carlton and St. Regis to Courtyard and Fairfield; Ritz-Carlton ranked highest of 104 brands in J.D. Power's 2026 North America Hotel Guest Satisfaction Study.

Hotel owners sign long franchise and management contracts (often 20 years or more) and invest in brand-specific design, so changing flags is costly; guests' Bonvoy points and elite status also make them reluctant to switch.

Marriott Bonvoy grew to nearly 271 million members at end-2025 (adding about 43 million in the year) and more than 295 million by mid-2026; more hotels make the program more valuable to members, and more members make the brand more valuable to owners.

With about 1.81 million rooms in 10,082 properties at June 30, 2026, Marriott spreads reservation, technology, sales and marketing costs over the largest system in the industry, lowering distribution costs for owners.
Hotel markets are open to new supply and many brands; only a handful of global systems can compete for owners, but local markets are not natural monopolies.

Its asset-light fee model is now copied by Hilton, IHG, Hyatt and Wyndham, so it no longer gives a unique edge; Marriott is responding to Airbnb with Homes & Villas and Apartments rather than counter-positioning it.
Nearly 100 years of hotel operating standards, revenue management and a culture of 'putting people first' (Fortune No. 7 Best Workplace in 2026) are hard for newcomers to replicate.
Its record pipeline of 4,186 properties and about 629,000 rooms (mid-2026, 44% under construction) and long-term owner contracts secure future locations and fees that rivals cannot take.

customers.evidence: Bonvoy membership rose from about 228 million at end-2024 to more than 295 million by mid-2026, and Ritz-Carlton topped J.D. Power's 2026 North America hotel satisfaction study; however, many frequent travelers complain online about Bonvoy point devaluations and inconsistent elite benefits.

talent.evidence: Marriott was named No. 7 on the 2026 Fortune and Great Place To Work 100 Best Workplaces list and has been on the list since its inception nearly three decades ago, with nearly 800,000 associates worldwide.

product.evidence: It has the broadest brand range of any hotel company, and Ritz-Carlton ranked highest of 104 brands benchmarked in J.D. Power's 2026 study, while rivals lead some segments (Tru by Hilton in midscale, Drury in upscale).

competitors.name: Hilton Worldwide Holdings
competitors.note: Closest global rival: 1.35 million rooms and 243 million Hilton Honors members, competing brand-for-brand from Waldorf Astoria to Hampton and Tru.

competitors.name: InterContinental Hotels Group
competitors.note: Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza, InterContinental and Kimpton compete in midscale to luxury worldwide, especially in Greater China and Europe.

competitors.name: Hyatt Hotels
competitors.note: Luxury, lifestyle and all-inclusive rival (Park Hyatt, Grand Hyatt, Andaz, Playa) with World of Hyatt loyalty; 372,763 rooms at end-2025.

competitors.note: Fast-growing Chinese chain (Hanting, JI Hotel, Steigenberger) competing with Marriott's select-service brands in China.

competitors.name: Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts
competitors.note: Private ultra-luxury operator competing with Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis and Bulgari for owners and high-end guests.

competitors.note: Private group competing in Europe, Middle East, Africa and Asia-Pacific upscale and midscale.

competitors.note: Online travel agency that controls much of hotel distribution; competes with Marriott for the customer relationship and direct bookings.

Jin Jiang International (not an SEC filer; figures not checked)
Minor International (not an SEC filer; figures not checked)

marketShare.market: Hotel rooms of the world's 10 largest hotel groups (HOTELS magazine 2026 ranking; share of the top-10 total)

threats: Hilton is growing its system faster (6.7% net unit growth in 2025 vs Marriott's 4.3%) and wins many conversion and midscale deals.
Weak U.S. & Canada RevPAR (+0.7% in 2025) and an economic slowdown would cut fees, especially incentive fees.
Chinese chains (H World, Jin Jiang, Atour) are taking share in China, where international RevPAR fell 0.5% in Q2 2026.
Airbnb and other alternative accommodations compete for leisure and group travelers.
Online travel agencies and AI booking assistants could weaken direct booking and loyalty economics.
Bonvoy point devaluations and inconsistent service at franchised hotels could erode guest loyalty.
High leverage: about $16.2 billion of debt and a $3.8 billion shareholders' deficit at end-2025 from heavy buybacks.
Cybersecurity: the 2018 Starwood guest database breach led to regulatory settlements and reputational harm.

ceo.name: Anthony (Tony) Capuano
ceo.background: Cornell University School of Hotel Administration graduate (1987); joined Marriott in 1995 and spent most of his career in hotel development, leading global development before becoming CEO

c1.evidence: Marriott leads the global hotel industry with about 1.81 million rooms (mid-2026), but lodging is a mature industry growing mid-single digits (net rooms +4.3% in 2025), not an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Guests choose it for the Bonvoy program (more than 295 million members), the widest brand range and consistent standards, and owners choose it for higher direct bookings; this scale is very hard to copy and should last many years.

c3.evidence: Marriott, Ritz-Carlton and Sheraton are household names and Marriott is the largest hotel company in the world; Ritz-Carlton ranked highest of 104 brands in J.D. Power's 2026 study.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'Connecting People Through The Power of Travel' and Serve 360 program are emphasized, but management is judged mainly on fee growth, RevPAR and over $4 billion of yearly capital returns.

c6.evidence: “reliable, big, business travel, Bonvoy points” come to mind; the impression is mostly positive, though frequent travelers often criticize Bonvoy devaluations and the 2018 Starwood data breach.

c7.evidence: Global travel is a huge market riding rising middle-class travel in Asia, the Middle East and India (Marriott's pipeline reached about 629,000 rooms by mid-2026), but growth is GDP-plus rather than a technology-driven secular boom.

c8.evidence: It keeps expanding into new segments such as midscale (City Express, Four Points Flex, Series by Marriott), citizenM, Apartments, outdoor lodging and Homes & Villas, but it remains in lodging.

m1.evidence: Capuano has pushed clear strategies such as midscale expansion, conversion brands and growth in India and the Middle East, but he is a disciplined operator rather than a visionary redefining travel.

m2.evidence: As a 30-year Marriott veteran he guards the founding Marriott family culture, but he is a hired professional CEO rather than a founder.

m4.evidence: Capuano frames leadership around associates, saying the goal is 'creating a culture rooted in trust, opportunity, and respect for every associate', and Marriott ranked No. 7 on Fortune's 2026 100 Best Workplaces list.

m5.evidence: Marriott's 'put people first' culture is strong and distinctive, but innovation is mainly new brands and a long-running technology modernization rather than a stream of new technologies.

m6.evidence: Capuano's background is hotel development and real estate, not engineering or technology.

m7.evidence: He is regarded as a steady, values-driven steward of the Marriott culture, with Serve 360 sustainability and human-trafficking-awareness programs, but there is no sign of a mission beyond responsible business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement address by Capuano at a top university was found; he has spoken at Cornell's Nolan School of Hotel Administration speaker series.

m8b.evidence: Capuano is a low-profile, conventional corporate leader, not a celebrity personality.

m9.evidence: Since 2021 revenue rose from $13,857 million (2021) to $26,186 million (2025), the system passed 10,000 properties, and $3.3 billion of shares were bought back in 2025 alone.

m10.evidence: The asset-light model keeps capital spending modest ($604 million in 2025), but Marriott is not known for a culture of frugality.

c10.evidence: Its hotels host hundreds of millions of guest stays a year in 145 countries and territories, but hotels are a convenience that many rivals can supply.

p2.evidence: Running a 10,000-hotel global brand and loyalty system is operationally hard to replicate, but hotels are not a frontier technology and the world would find alternatives.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 0.8% in pandemic-hit 2020 to 16.7% in 2022 but has since been flat to lower (16.3% in 2023, 15.0% in 2024, 15.8% in 2025); gross margin is not reported.

f3.evidence: At end-2025 total debt was $16,204 million versus $358 million of cash and $3,212 million of operating cash flow, and shareholders' equity was a $3,771 million deficit due to buybacks.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $84 million (2020) to $4,141 million (2025) and operating cash flow from $1,639 million to $3,212 million, but both dipped in 2024 (operating income $3,767M, cash flow $2,749M).

v1.evidence: Marriott offers the most hotels and the biggest loyalty program, a practical reason to choose it, but Hilton offers a comparable experience and leads guest satisfaction in some segments.

v2.evidence: Marriott ranked No. 7 on the 2026 Fortune and Great Place To Work 100 Best Workplaces in the U.S. and has appeared on the list every year since it began nearly three decades ago.

c5.evidence: Hotel owners, its nearly 800,000 associates and loyal Bonvoy travelers would miss it, but guests could stay at Hilton, Hyatt or Airbnb instead, so the world would adapt.
